alt: Power, getting your own way even against resistance, takes two forms. Authority is accepted as legitimate, as when pupils accept a teacher’s right to ask for quiet, and is stable. Coercion rests on force or fear, as when a bully takes a phone, and is costly to maintain.
caption: Authority is power people accept as rightful; coercion is power based on fear.

alt: A table comparing traditional, charismatic and rational-legal authority: why people obey, examples, strengths and weaknesses. Traditional authority is stable but resists change; charismatic authority inspires but is unstable; rational-legal authority is predictable but can become rigid red tape.
caption: Each type of authority gains legitimacy in a different way, and can lose it in a different way.

alt: A chain: a charismatic leader with devoted followers faces a crisis when the leader fails or dies; followers set up an organisation, rules or a line of succession; the authority becomes lasting rules or traditions.
caption: Charisma is unstable, so followers turn it into rules or traditions.

alt: A pyramid of offices, each supervised by the one above, beside a list of features: hierarchy, written rules, specialisation, impersonality, and appointment on qualifications and merit. Bureaucracy is the organisational form of rational-legal authority, found in government departments, companies, hospitals and schools.
caption: Bureaucracy puts rational-legal authority into practice through rules and a hierarchy of offices.

alt: Four cards. Functionalists say power serves society through value consensus. Marxists say it serves the ruling class through ideology. Feminists say men dominate formal and informal power. Pluralists say power is spread among competing groups. Each card ends with a criticism.
caption: The perspectives disagree about whether authority in the UK is genuinely legitimate.

after: ## Worked example: applying Weber to an item
alt: A fictional item about a mosque. The imam’s influence is charismatic and informal, because people follow his personal qualities and no rule obliges them. The treasurer holds rational-legal, formal authority, because she is elected under a written constitution and a successor would inherit the same authority.
caption: Name the type, link it to the item, and explain why it fits.
